lessons.summary: If the input is "0", which result is displayed?
explanation: InvalidMinutes is a custom error type. Deriving Debug supports diagnostic formatting; implementing Display supplies the user-facing message. lessons.title: Box and recursive ownership
lessons.summary: If the second stored value changes from 4 to 9, what is the sum?
explanation: A recursive enum cannot contain another full copy of itself directly with no indirection. Box<List> stores an owning pointer to a heap-allocated List, giving the enum a finite representation. Dropping the box releases its owned allocation and nested values.

The tiny list owns a tail through Box. Matching &self borrows each node; n and tail are borrowed values, and the sum method reads them without taking ownership. The example uses two nodes only: recursive processing and recursive destruction are not a promise of unlimited stack capacity.
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Rc and shared single-thread ownership
lessons.summary: If second is instead a new independent Rc allocation, what counts does first report?
explanation: Rc<T> is a reference-counted pointer for shared ownership within one thread. Rc::clone adds another strong owner of the same allocation. It does not clone the String itself. Rc::strong_count reports the current strong owner count in this controlled example.

drop(second) consumes and drops that owner now rather than waiting for its enclosing scope to end. The allocation remains while a strong owner exists. Rc uses non-atomic reference counts and is not Send or Sync; do not use it to share ownership across threads. Strong reference cycles can prevent reclamation; Weak is a separate tool for breaking those cycles.

Expected output or behavior: 2
1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: RefCell and runtime borrow checks
lessons.summary: If the shared guard is dropped before try_borrow_mut, what is printed?
explanation: RefCell permits interior mutability through a shared reference, while enforcing the usual one-mutable-or-many-shared borrow rule at runtime. borrow and borrow_mut panic if the rule is violated; try_borrow_mut instead returns a Result so a conflict can be handled without a panic.

The value returned by borrow is a guard. While read remains alive, a mutable borrow cannot be granted. Explicitly dropping it ends that shared borrow, allowing the later mutable guard to change the value. RefCell is not a thread synchronization primitive.

lessons.title: Arc and shared thread-safe ownership
lessons.summary: If other is a separate Arc::new(7) rather than a clone, what is printed?

lessons.title: Send Sync and type boundaries
lessons.summary: If this example uses Rc instead of Arc, what happens?
explanation: Send means a value’s ownership may be transferred between threads; Sync means sharing &T between threads is safe. These are marker traits, usually derived automatically from a type’s contents. Do not write unsafe implementations merely to suppress a compiler error.

The correct repair depends on ownership and access needs, not just silencing a diagnostic.

lessons.summary: With no user argument, what prints?
explanation: std::env::args yields Unicode command-line argument Strings. skip(1) omits the conventional program-name entry, then collect::<Vec<String>> stores the user arguments. If non-Unicode arguments must be supported, use args_os instead; args can panic on invalid Unicode.

Run this example as ./app read for the worked output. A slice pattern [topic] matches exactly one argument, borrowing that String. The fallback handles zero or several user arguments without indexing a missing item. This is an application policy, not shell parsing implemented by Rust.
Expected output or behavior: topic=read. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Parsing and validation policy
lessons.summary: If the input changes to "61", what is returned to the display branch?
explanation: parse::<u32> checks whether text is a representable unsigned integer. It does not know whether a study session should permit zero or a very large duration. trim deliberately accepts leading and trailing whitespace; that normalization is part of the chosen policy.

The helper returns a descriptive Result after enforcing 1 through 60. This sample uses static string error messages, so no owned error allocation is needed. The success branch receives only a validated minute count; parse failure and range failure remain distinguishable.

lessons.title: Formatting and Display
lessons.summary: If minutes becomes 20, what does the same Display implementation produce?
explanation: Implementing fmt::Display lets {} format a type. The fmt method borrows self and a mutable Formatter, then returns fmt::Result. The placeholder lifetime '_ means the compiler infers the borrow lifetime; it is not a new stored lifetime parameter on Session.

write!(f, ...) sends output to the caller’s formatter and returns any formatting error. The trailing expression returns that Result directly. Debug and Display serve different purposes; deriving Debug does not create this Display representation.
Expected output or behavior: 15 min. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Async futures and execution boundaries
lessons.summary: If drop(future) is replaced by future.await in this ordinary main, what happens?
explanation: An async block produces a Future value describing work. Its body progresses only when the future is polled. Creating the future does not spawn a thread, start a timer or install an executor. This example deliberately drops an unpolled future.

The .await syntax is allowed inside an async function or block, not this ordinary main. An executor is responsible for polling and wakeups for general asynchronous work. No Tokio or other runtime is used here; the next lesson polls only an already-ready standard-library future once, not arbitrary I/O.
Expected output or behavior: created. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why writing async alone provides neither a thread nor a general I/O runtime. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Pin Poll and a ready future
lessons.summary: If ready is constructed with 11, what does the one poll produce?
explanation: Future::poll takes a pinned mutable receiver and a task Context, returning Poll::Ready(value) or Poll::Pending. Box::pin constructs a pinned heap value; as_mut reborrows it as Pin<&mut _>. Pin supports address-stability contracts for types that require them, not a blanket ban on moving every Rust value.

future::ready returns a future guaranteed to produce Ready on its poll. Waker::noop ignores wake requests, so it cannot drive general futures that become ready later. Context::from_waker supplies that waker for this single bounded poll. Never turn this into a spin loop or poll the completed future again; this is not a general executor.
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why replacing ready with a timer future would require real wakeup scheduling rather than this no-op waker. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Declarative macros and expansion
lessons.summary: If the expansion becomes ($value) + ($value), what prints?
explanation: macro_rules! defines syntax patterns. In ($value:expr), $value captures one expression; the expansion uses it in ordinary Rust code. The ! at a call site distinguishes macro invocation from a normal function call.

This twice macro binds the captured expression once to a local value, then uses that value twice. The input block increments calls and returns three. Duplicating $value in two evaluated positions instead would evaluate the input twice; a macro does not automatically guarantee single evaluation.
Expected output or behavior: 6 1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Unsafe contracts and safe interfaces
lessons.summary: If the requested index is 1, what does the safe access produce?
explanation: Unsafe operations have conditions the programmer must uphold when the compiler cannot verify them. An unsafe block does not disable borrowing rules everywhere, make invalid memory valid or turn undefined behavior into a predictable demonstration. Safe public wrappers must enforce their own invariants before relying on unsafe internals.

slice.get returns an Option after checking the index, so this example needs no unsafe block at all. By contrast, get_unchecked requires a valid in-bounds index even if its result is not later used. We do not call it with an invalid index or execute any undefined-behavior example.
Expected output or behavior: missing. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: A bounded study-session pipeline
lessons.summary: If the first text changes to "70", what is collected and summed?
explanation: This fixed array contains four text inputs. parse::<u32>().ok() converts a parse Result to an Option, and filter_map keeps only Some values. The range filter then keeps minute counts from 1 through 60. This intentionally skips invalid inputs rather than misrepresenting them as valid zero-minute sessions.

take(2) keeps at most two accepted values. collect builds a Vec<u32>, and iter().sum::<u32>() totals its borrowed elements. Since each retained value is at most sixty, the total is bounded by 120. This is an in-memory teaching pipeline, not durable storage or a complete error-reporting application.

Expected output or behavior: [15, 20]
35. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
